docs.title: Technical Writer | Engineering Documentation | API Documentation
docs.text:
I turn complex technical information into clear, accurate, and user-focused documentation.

With hands-on experience in oil and gas engineering and wellhead services, I understand the importance of technical accuracy, structured procedures, equipment documentation, troubleshooting guidance, and safety-conscious communication.

I combine this engineering background with practical documentation-as-code skills using Markdown, MkDocs, GitHub, and OpenAPI to create organized, maintainable technical content.

Areas of focus: Engineering documentation · Technical procedures · Equipment guides · API documentation · Documentation-as-code

docs.title: How I Approach Documentation
docs.text:
1. Understand the audience — identify the reader, their task, and the information they need.
  2. Organize the content — structure information with consistent headings, terminology, tables, and examples.
  3. Write clearly — make technical concepts easier to understand without losing important detail.
  4. Verify the content — check links, formatting, examples, and consistency against available source information.
  5. Maintain the documentation — use version control and repeatable publishing workflows where appropriate.

docs.title: Wellhead Installation Documentation — 10,000 psi Multi-Bowl Wellhead System
docs.text: Portfolio sample — illustrative documentation only. This document demonstrates technical writing structure and documentation practices. It is not an approved field procedure. Installation activities, connection methods, pressure-test requirements, and acceptance criteria must be verified against the exact equipment manufacturer's instructions, approved well program, and applicable site procedures before use.

docs.title: 1. Document Control
docs.text: Field Details Document Title Illustrative; not approved for field execution Document ID SOP-OPS-WH-10K-001 Version 2.0 — Portfolio Sample Effective Date October 2026 Equipment Reference Illustrative multi-bowl wellhead system; exact manufacturer and model to be verified against approved equipment documentation Author Ikechukwu Okonkwo — Portfolio Documentation Sample Document Status Illustrative; not approved for field execution

docs.title: 2.1 Objective
docs.text: This document demonstrates how a wellhead installation activity can be organized into a structured technical procedure covering preparation, equipment inspection, installation planning, connection verification, testing documentation, troubleshooting, and handover.

docs.title: 2.2 Scope
docs.text:
The sample addresses documentation for an API 10,000 psi-rated multi-bowl wellhead system intended to accommodate multiple casing strings within a compact wellhead arrangement, subject to the specific manufacturer's design.

The actual equipment configuration, pressure ratings, casing program, connection type, installation sequence, and testing requirements must be confirmed before an operational procedure is issued.

docs.title: 2.3 Intended Audience
docs.text: This document is intended for: - Drilling and completions engineers - Wellhead installation personnel - Field service engineers - HSE personnel - Quality assurance and quality control personnel - Technical documentation reviewers

docs.title: 3. HSE Requirements and Hazards
docs.text: Critical safety notice: This sample does not authorize field work. All work must be performed under the applicable approved work procedures, risk assessments, Permit to Work (PTW) requirements, and site-specific HSE controls. Pressure isolation, verification of well status, lifting operations, and any hot work must be managed by competent and authorized personnel.

docs.title: 3.1 Key Hazards
docs.text: Hazard Potential Consequence Required Control Approach Suspended loads Crushing injuries, dropped objects, or equipment damage Use an approved lifting plan, certified lifting equipment, and designated exclusion zones Trapped pressure Uncontrolled release of fluids or energy Verify isolation and zero-energy status using approved site procedures Hot work Fire, burns, or ignition of flammable materials Apply the approved hot-work procedure and required gas-testing controls Stored hydraulic energy Injection injuries or uncontrolled equipment movement Follow the equipment manufacturer's isolation and depressurization instructions Manual handling Strains, impact injuries, or hand injuries Use suitable handling aids and task-specific controls Incorrect equipment configuration Seal failure, connection damage, or loss of containment Verify equipment identification, ratings, compatibility, and approved installation documentation

docs.title: 3.2 Personal Protective Equipment
docs.text:
PPE must be selected through the approved risk assessment and site requirements. Depending on the task, this may include:

  • Safety helmet
  • Safety glasses or approved eye protection
  • Safety footwear
  • Suitable protective coveralls
  • Task-appropriate gloves
  • Hearing protection where required
  • Welding helmet and protective clothing for authorized hot work

PPE does not replace engineering controls, isolation, lifting controls, or other required safeguards.

docs.title: 4. Required Tools and Equipment
docs.text:
The following list is a preliminary documentation checklist. Final selection and suitability must be confirmed against the approved equipment list and manufacturer's instructions.

  • [ ] Correctly identified multi-bowl wellhead housing with verified ratings
  • [ ] Approved casing preparation and cutting equipment
  • [ ] Manufacturer-approved running, landing, and handling tools
  • [ ] Certified lifting equipment and suitable lifting accessories
  • [ ] Calibrated torque equipment, where applicable to the specified connection
  • [ ] Approved pressure-testing equipment and suitable instrumentation
  • [ ] Required seals and sealing components, verified against the equipment bill of materials
  • [ ] Inspection and dimensional measurement tools
  • [ ] Required non-destructive testing (NDT) equipment and qualified personnel, where specified
  • [ ] Approved drawings, equipment data sheets, installation instructions, and test procedures
  • [ ] Current calibration certificates and inspection records, as applicable

Verification note: Do not assume that equipment with a nominal 10,000 psi rating, a particular torque capacity, or a particular seal type is suitable for every configuration. Confirm the applicable ratings, connections, tools, and acceptance criteria before work begins.

docs.title: 5. Installation Workflow
docs.text: The following stages provide a documentation framework. The detailed execution steps and mandatory hold points must come from the approved installation procedure for the specific wellhead assembly.

docs.title: Step 1: Preparation and Casing Verification
docs.text:
Objective: Confirm that the installation can proceed using the correct equipment, approved references, and verified casing information.

Documentation and verification requirements:

  1. Confirm the approved well program, work pack, and applicable risk assessments are available.
  2. Verify the equipment model, serial number, pressure rating, connection details, and compatibility with the casing program.
  3. Confirm the required well-status and isolation checks have been completed by authorized personnel.
  4. Verify casing dimensions, condition, reference measurements, and preparation requirements against the approved drawings.
  5. Record the inspection results and resolve discrepancies before proceeding.

Hold point: Installation must not proceed until required well-status checks, equipment identification, and casing acceptance criteria have been verified and authorized.

docs.title: Step 2: Equipment Inspection and Seal Verification
docs.text:
Objective: Confirm that the equipment and sealing components are correct and suitable for the specified assembly.

Inspection checklist:

  • [ ] Equipment identification and serial numbers recorded
  • [ ] Pressure ratings and connection specifications verified
  • [ ] Relevant sealing surfaces inspected against manufacturer acceptance criteria
  • [ ] Seals and sealing components checked against the approved parts list
  • [ ] Components inspected for visible damage, corrosion, or contamination
  • [ ] Required lubricants and assembly materials verified against manufacturer instructions
  • [ ] Inspection findings recorded and reviewed

Damaged, unidentified, incompatible, or nonconforming components must be referred for technical disposition in accordance with the approved quality process.

docs.title: Step 3: Lifting, Positioning, and Alignment
docs.text:
Objective: Document the controlled positioning of the wellhead assembly.

  1. Verify that the approved lifting plan and equipment requirements have been satisfied.
  2. Confirm that the handling tools and lifting points are suitable for the identified assembly.
  3. Record the equipment orientation and alignment requirements specified in the approved drawings.
  4. Verify the assembly position and alignment using the manufacturer's specified acceptance criteria and suitable measurement methods.
  5. Record inspection results and resolve any discrepancy before the next authorized stage.

Hold point: Do not accept the assembly based solely on visual alignment or a spirit-level reading. Use the acceptance criteria specified for the actual equipment configuration.

docs.title: Step 4: Connection Installation and Verification
docs.text:
Objective: Confirm that the specified connection is installed in accordance with the applicable manufacturer's instructions.

The connection method must be established from the approved equipment configuration. Welding, slip-on, set-screw, and other connection arrangements are not interchangeable unless the manufacturer and approved engineering documentation explicitly permit the selected configuration.

Verification requirements:

  • Confirm the specified connection type and applicable drawings.
  • Verify that the required joining procedure and qualified personnel are available.
  • Confirm that applicable materials, consumables, and tools meet the approved requirements.
  • Record required inspection, dimensional verification, and NDT results, where applicable.
  • Verify completion of the specified acceptance checks before proceeding.

Important: Welding parameters, preheat requirements, torque values, tightening sequences, and other connection-specific instructions must be taken from the applicable approved procedure. They must not be inferred from this portfolio sample.

docs.title: Step 5: Pressure Testing and Acceptance
docs.text:
Objective: Document the approved test requirements, execution records, and acceptance decision for the installed assembly.

The test method, test medium, pressure stages, hold times, boundaries, and acceptance criteria depend on the specific equipment, connection, applicable standards, and approved test procedure.

Before testing, verify that:

  • The approved test procedure and equipment limits are available.
  • The test boundary and components included in the test are clearly identified.
  • Required instruments are suitable and within calibration.
  • Isolation, exclusion zones, communication, and pressure-release controls are established.
  • The test is authorized and supervised by competent personnel.

Record the following information:

Test Record Field Required Information Equipment identification Equipment description, model, and serial number Approved test procedure Document number and revision Test boundary Components and connections included Test medium As specified in the approved procedure Test stages Approved pressure values and hold times Instrumentation Instrument IDs and calibration details Observations Recorded pressure, duration, leakage observations, and relevant findings Acceptance criteria Criteria defined by the approved procedure Final result Pass, fail, or pending technical review Authorization Names, roles, signatures, and date of authorized reviewers

Acceptance rule: Do not use the pressure values or hold times in the original draft as approved test requirements. Confirm all values and acceptance criteria against the applicable manufacturer documentation and approved test procedure. Any failure must be managed through the approved depressurization, investigation, corrective-action, and retesting process.

docs.title: 6. Contingency and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The table below provides a documentation framework for recording discrepancies. Corrective actions must be approved for the actual equipment and operating conditions.

Issue Possible Cause Required Response Pressure-test failure Seal damage, connection defect, equipment malfunction, or test-system issue Stop the test in accordance with the approved procedure; secure the system and investigate before corrective work Alignment outside acceptance criteria Dimensional discrepancy, casing preparation issue, or positioning error Suspend progression and request engineering review against the approved drawings and tolerances Connection or fastener discrepancy Incorrect components, damaged threads, or assembly outside specification Stop and refer to the manufacturer's instructions and approved corrective-action process Seal damage or contamination Improper handling, incompatible materials, or surface defects Quarantine the affected components and obtain an approved inspection and disposition Missing equipment traceability Incomplete identification or documentation Resolve the traceability gap before equipment acceptance Incomplete test records Missing readings, calibration details, or authorization Hold final acceptance until the required records are completed and reviewed

All discrepancies should be recorded with a unique reference, description, responsible person, corrective action, and closure evidence.

docs.title: 7. Quality Records and Sign-Off
docs.text: The installation documentation package should include the applicable records required by the approved work pack.

docs.title: 7.1 Close-Out Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Equipment model, serial numbers, and identification recorded
  • [ ] Approved drawings and equipment specifications referenced
  • [ ] Inspection and dimensional verification records completed
  • [ ] Applicable connection inspection and NDT reports attached
  • [ ] Pressure-test records and supporting charts attached, where required
  • [ ] Instrument calibration records referenced
  • [ ] Nonconformances and corrective actions closed or formally dispositioned
  • [ ] Required inspection and acceptance points signed off
  • [ ] Handover package reviewed by the designated authority

docs.title: 7.2 Sign-Off Record
docs.text:
Role Name Signature Date Field Engineer Wellhead Service Representative QA/QC Representative, where required Drilling or Completions Supervisor

Final approval must be provided by the personnel designated in the approved project documentation. This portfolio sample does not constitute operational authorization.

docs.title: 8. References and Technical Verification
docs.text:
Before this document is adapted for operational use, identify and verify the applicable revisions of:

  • Manufacturer's installation, operation, and maintenance instructions for the exact wellhead model
  • Approved well program and casing design
  • Applicable API Specification 6A requirements, including the relevant edition and addenda, and the project-specific pressure-rating and equipment requirements, where applicable.
  • Approved connection, welding, inspection, and NDT procedures, where applicable
  • Approved pressure-testing procedure and acceptance criteria
  • Site HSE requirements, lifting plan, and Permit to Work documentation
  • Project quality plan and equipment traceability requirements

The applicable documents, revisions, and acceptance criteria must be recorded in the controlled operational version.

docs.title: Portfolio Disclaimer
docs.text: This document is an illustrative technical writing sample. Equipment descriptions and installation topics are included to demonstrate document organization, technical communication, inspection records, and quality documentation. The content has not been validated as a manufacturer-approved procedure. It must not be used to execute field work without review, technical verification, and formal approval by the responsible engineering authority.

docs.title: Technical Troubleshooting and Maintenance Documentation Guide
1. Introduction
docs.text:
This guide demonstrates how technical troubleshooting information can be organized to help engineers, technicians, and maintenance personnel identify equipment problems, investigate possible causes, document findings, and determine appropriate next steps.

It uses a general industrial equipment example to demonstrate technical writing practices. It is not a substitute for equipment-specific troubleshooting instructions or an approved maintenance procedure.

docs.title: Document Information
docs.text: Field Details Document Title Technical Troubleshooting and Maintenance Documentation Guide Document Type Illustrative technical writing sample Author Ikechukwu Okonkwo Version 1.0 Document Status Portfolio sample; not an approved operational procedure

docs.title: 2. Purpose
docs.text:
The purpose of this guide is to demonstrate a consistent approach to technical troubleshooting by helping readers:

  • Identify and describe equipment symptoms.
  • Gather relevant operating and maintenance information.
  • Investigate possible causes systematically.
  • Record inspection findings and corrective actions.
  • Verify the outcome and maintain accurate maintenance records.

docs.title: 3. Scope
docs.text:
This guide provides a general framework for troubleshooting industrial equipment and instrumentation.

Actual troubleshooting activities must follow the applicable manufacturer's documentation, site procedures, risk assessment, and authorization requirements.

docs.title: 4. Safety Precautions
docs.text:
Before investigating an equipment problem:

  • Review the applicable risk assessment and work instructions.
  • Obtain the required work authorization.
  • Identify electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, and process-energy hazards.
  • Apply approved isolation and lockout/tagout procedures where required.
  • Verify the equipment is in a safe condition before inspection.
  • Use appropriate personal protective equipment.
  • Ensure only competent and authorized personnel perform technical tests and repairs.

Warning: Never loosen pressurized fittings, open process connections, bypass safety devices, or work on energized equipment unless an approved procedure specifically permits the activity and the required safeguards are in place.

docs.title: Step 1: Describe the Problem
docs.text:
Record the reported symptom as clearly and objectively as possible.

Examples include:

  • Equipment fails to start.
  • An instrument reading appears inconsistent.
  • A system generates an alarm.
  • Equipment performance differs from the expected operating condition.
  • A component shows visible damage or leakage.

Record the date, equipment identification, operating conditions, alarm codes, and circumstances under which the problem occurred, where available.

docs.title: Step 2: Review Available Information
docs.text:
Review relevant technical information before deciding on corrective action.

This may include:

  • Equipment manuals and technical data sheets
  • Electrical or instrumentation drawings
  • Previous maintenance reports
  • Alarm and event logs
  • Inspection records
  • Calibration certificates
  • Approved operating procedures

Confirm that the documentation applies to the actual equipment model and configuration.

docs.title: Step 3: Identify Possible Causes
docs.text:
Develop a list of potential causes based on the observed symptoms and available evidence.

Observed Symptom Potential Cause Information to Review Equipment does not start Power supply, control signal, interlock, or mechanical issue Electrical drawings, alarm history, and approved start-up procedure Instrument reading is unstable Sensor issue, loose connection, interference, or changing process conditions Instrument specification, signal records, and calibration history Unexpected alarm Operating condition outside configured limits or instrument fault Alarm log, configured limits, and equipment documentation Reduced equipment performance Operating conditions, wear, blockage, or control issue Performance history, inspection records, and manufacturer guidance Visible leakage Seal, fitting, connection, or component damage Equipment drawings, inspection history, and approved isolation procedure

these causes are not confirmed diagnoses. The actual cause must be established through appropriate inspection and testing.

docs.title: Step 4: Investigate and Record Findings
docs.text:
Follow the approved troubleshooting procedure for the specific equipment.

Record:

  • The checks performed
  • The instruments and tools used
  • Relevant readings and observations
  • Any alarm codes or error messages
  • Deviations from the expected condition
  • The evidence supporting or ruling out each suspected cause

Do not make assumptions where measurements or inspection evidence are unavailable.

docs.title: Step 5: Determine the Corrective Action
docs.text:
Select corrective action based on verified findings, equipment requirements, and the applicable maintenance procedure.

Depending on the findings, the next step may involve further diagnosis, adjustment by authorized personnel, component replacement, calibration, repair, or escalation to the manufacturer or responsible engineering team.

Record the approved action and the person or team responsible for carrying it out.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Outcome
docs.text:
After authorized corrective work is completed:

  1. Confirm that required inspections and checks have been completed.
  2. Verify that the equipment is reassembled and restored in accordance with the applicable procedure.
  3. Perform the prescribed functional or operational checks.
  4. Compare the results with the approved acceptance criteria.
  5. Record the outcome and any outstanding issues.
  6. Return the equipment to service only after the required authorization has been obtained.

If the problem remains unresolved, document the outstanding symptoms and escalate the issue through the approved technical support process.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting Report Template
docs.text:
Use the following template to demonstrate consistent technical recordkeeping.

Field Information to Record Report reference Unique report or work-order number Equipment identification Equipment name, tag number, model, and serial number, where applicable Date and time When the issue was reported and investigated Reported symptom Description of the observed problem Operating conditions Relevant conditions at the time of the issue Initial assessment Preliminary observations and potential causes Investigation performed Checks, measurements, and inspections completed Findings Evidence collected during the investigation Root cause Confirmed cause, if established Corrective action Approved repair or action taken Verification results Results against the applicable acceptance criteria Final status Resolved, unresolved, or awaiting further investigation Prepared and reviewed by Names, roles, and dates

docs.title: 7. Example Troubleshooting Record
docs.text:
The following is an illustrative example showing how a troubleshooting report can present findings without claiming an unverified diagnosis.

Reported issue: An industrial pressure indicator displays a fluctuating reading.

Initial assessment: The cause has not been confirmed.

Investigation plan: - Review the instrument specification and installation documentation. - Compare the displayed reading with available operating records. - Check for relevant alarms and recent maintenance activity. - Arrange inspection and testing by an authorized technician in accordance with the approved procedure.

Finding: Pending inspection and verification.

Corrective action: To be determined from the investigation results.

Verification: The instrument must be assessed against the applicable manufacturer requirements and approved acceptance criteria before the issue can be closed.

This example demonstrates the difference between a reported symptom, a suspected cause, a verified finding, and an approved corrective action.

docs.title: 8. Common Documentation Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following practices when preparing troubleshooting documentation:

  • Presenting a suspected cause as a confirmed diagnosis.
  • Recording measurements without units or relevant operating context.
  • Recommending repairs without checking equipment-specific requirements.
  • Omitting equipment identification or document references.
  • Failing to record inspection results and corrective actions.
  • Closing a report without documenting verification results.
  • Using outdated drawings, manuals, or procedures.

Clear records improve traceability and help other personnel understand what was investigated and what remains unresolved.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
A structured troubleshooting process supports clear communication, evidence-based diagnosis, consistent maintenance records, and appropriate escalation of unresolved issues.

Effective technical documentation distinguishes symptoms from causes, records the evidence collected, identifies approved corrective actions, and documents verification before an issue is closed.

docs.title: 10. Important Notice
docs.text: This document is an illustrative technical writing sample for portfolio purposes. It does not provide equipment-specific repair instructions and must not be used as an operational procedure. Actual troubleshooting, maintenance, testing, and return-to-service activities must follow the applicable manufacturer documentation and approved site procedures.

docs.title: Wellhead Telemetry API Reference
docs.text:
This reference documents an illustrative REST API for retrieving wellhead telemetry data. It demonstrates API documentation practices for endpoint definitions, authentication, request parameters, JSON responses, error handling, and rate limits.

Demonstration API

This is a portfolio example, not a verified or deployed API. The base URL, credentials, responses, rate limits, and endpoint behaviour are illustrative. Requests will not retrieve live well data. Do not use these examples for operational or safety-critical decisions.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: The example API represents a service that provides telemetry readings associated with a wellhead monitoring system.

docs.title: Intended audience
docs.text:
• Software developers integrating telemetry data into an application
  • Technical teams reviewing a monitoring API
  • Engineers and documentation specialists evaluating the example interface

docs.title: Example capabilities
docs.text:
• Request telemetry for a specified rig
  • Review pressure and temperature readings
  • Inspect the reported telemetry status
  • Handle invalid requests and authentication errors

docs.title: 2. Base URL
docs.text:
The reserved .invalid domain is used to prevent the example from being mistaken for a live service.

https://api.example.invalid
Property Description API style REST Data format JSON Example API version v1 Authentication model Bearer token Transport HTTPS in the illustrative design

docs.title: 3. Authentication
docs.text:
The example uses a Bearer token in the HTTP Authorization header.

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_EXAMPLE_TOKEN

YOUR_EXAMPLE_TOKEN is a placeholder, not a working credential. This portfolio example does not provide a token issuance or validation service.

docs.title: Authentication requirements
docs.text:
• Include the token in the Authorization header.
  • Do not place credentials in query parameters.
  • Avoid committing real credentials to source control.
  • A real implementation should use an approved token provisioning and rotation process.

An unauthenticated or invalidly authenticated request is illustrated as returning 401 Unauthorized.

docs.title: 4. Retrieve Telemetry
docs.text: Returns an illustrative telemetry record for the requested rig.

docs.title: GET /v1/sensors/telemetry
docs.text:
Purpose: Retrieve an example telemetry record associated with a specified rig.

Authentication: Bearer token, as described in Section 3.

docs.title: Request parameters
docs.text: Parameter Location Type Required Description rig_id Query String Yes Identifier of the rig whose telemetry is requested

docs.title: Example request
docs.text:
curl --get "https://api.example.invalid/v1/sensors/telemetry" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_EXAMPLE_TOKEN" \
  --header "Accept: application/json" \
  --data-urlencode "rig_id=RIG-001"

This command illustrates the request format only. The reserved host does not provide a live API service.

docs.title: Example successful response
docs.text:
Illustrative HTTP status: 200 OK

{
  "timestamp": "2026-10-20T10:30:00Z",
  "rig_id": "RIG-001",
  "pressure_psi": 1250.5,
  "temperature_f": 178.4,
  "status": "normal"
}

docs.title: Response fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description timestamp String (date-time) Example timestamp for the reading, represented in UTC rig_id String Identifier associated with the requested rig pressure_psi Number Illustrative pressure reading in pounds per square inch temperature_f Number Illustrative temperature reading in degrees Fahrenheit status String (enum) Illustrative status label. Possible example values are normal, warning, and unknown; these are not safety decisions or approved alarm thresholds.

The example values are fictional and do not represent actual operating conditions or approved alarm thresholds.

docs.title: 5. HTTP Status Codes and Error Handling
docs.text:
The following responses illustrate how a real implementation could communicate common request failures.

Status code Meaning Example cause 200 OK Request succeeded A telemetry record is returned 400 Bad Request Request is invalid Required rig_id is missing or malformed 401 Unauthorized Authentication failed Token is missing, invalid, or expired 429 Too Many Requests Rate limit exceeded Request quota has been exceeded

docs.title: Example error response
docs.text:
Illustrative HTTP status: 400 Bad Request

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INVALID_REQUEST",
    "message": "The rig_id query parameter is required."
  }
}

This is a proposed error format for the demonstration. It is not a confirmed response from a live service.

docs.title: Troubleshooting guidance
docs.text:
400 Bad Request

Check that rig_id is present, correctly spelled, and supplied as a query parameter.

401 Unauthorized

Check that the Authorization header uses the Bearer scheme and that a valid token has been supplied. This example does not issue or validate tokens.

429 Too Many Requests

Stop sending requests temporarily and follow the retry guidance provided by the actual service, if available. A production API should document whether it provides a Retry-After header and rate-limit headers.

docs.title: 6. Rate Limits
docs.text:
Rate limits define how many requests a client may make within a specified period.

This example does not establish a verified rate limit. Any quota documented for a real implementation must be confirmed with the service owner.

A production API should document:

  • The applicable quota and its time window
  • Whether limits apply per user, token, or API key
  • The response returned when a quota is exceeded
  • Any rate-limit headers and retry guidance

docs.title: 7. Request and Response Conventions
docs.text:
The example uses the following conventions:

  • HTTP methods describe the intended operation.
  • Query parameters identify the requested rig.
  • JSON represents the example response payload.
  • Bearer authentication is illustrated through an HTTP header.
  • HTTP status codes communicate success or failure.

A production implementation should also define field validation, timestamp guarantees, units, nullability, data freshness, and the meaning of each possible status value.

docs.title: 8. Security and Operational Considerations
docs.text:
Telemetry can inform engineering decisions, so a real implementation requires controls beyond documenting an endpoint.

  • Enforce HTTPS and secure credential handling.
  • Authenticate and authorize callers.
  • Validate request parameters.
  • Define monitoring, logging, and error-handling requirements.
  • Document data freshness and measurement units.
  • Establish appropriate access controls and retention policies.
  • Verify all behaviour against the deployed service and approved engineering requirements.

Important: This API example is not a control system and must not be used to operate equipment, determine safe operating limits, or replace approved field procedures.

docs.title: 9. Related Resources
docs.text:
• Home — Technical Documentation Portfolio
  • Wellhead Documentation
  • Technical Guide

docs.title: 10. Scope and Limitations
docs.text:
This reference demonstrates the structure and writing style of an API reference. It does not establish that an API implementation exists.

Before adapting this documentation for a real service, verify the base URL, authentication mechanism, endpoint behaviour, schemas, error responses, rate limits, and security requirements with the service owner and approved technical sources.
